intro.title: Welcome to the Indus Valley
intro.text: You are standing in a street of a city like Mohenjo-daro, as it may have looked around 4,500 years ago. The Indus Valley Civilization was one of the world's earliest urban cultures, with planned streets, baked-brick houses and covered drains.

hint.text: Walk with W A S D and look by dragging the mouse. Glowing signposts mark the five places you can explore.

enter.title: The Citadel of Mohenjo-daro
enter.text: Rising above the lower town, the citadel stood on a huge platform of mud and baked brick. Here lay the Great Bath, one of the best-preserved structures of the civilization. Use the tour for a guided walk, or explore on your own.

tour_approach.title: The approach
tour_approach.text: From the lower town, a brick stairway climbs the citadel platform. Raising the platform may have helped protect these buildings from floods, and it certainly made them stand out.

tour_overview.title: An overview
tour_overview.text: From above you can see the Great Bath at the centre, with the Granary to its west. Scholars still debate how the citadel's buildings were used, and the names we give them are modern.

tour_steps.title: The steps
tour_steps.text: Flights of brick steps lead down into the pool at both short ends. Low platforms beside them may have been used for resting or for changing.

tour_water.title: The water
tour_water.text: The pool is about 12 metres long, 7 metres wide and 2.4 metres deep. Water was probably carried in from a nearby well and let out through a drain in a corner of the pool.

tour_corridors.title: The corridors
tour_corridors.text: A brick corridor with a row of pillars ran around the pool. Rooms opened off it, and a staircase suggests an upper storey that has since been lost.

tour_granary.title: The 'Granary'
tour_granary.text: To the west stands a large raised brick platform called the Granary. Its true function is debated: it may have stored grain, but some scholars think it served another purpose.

hotspot_steps.title: Steps into the pool
hotspot_steps.text: Wide brick steps run down into the pool at both short ends, each reaching the full depth of 2.4 metres in a series of low risers. Their careful, even finish shows the builders' skill with baked brick.
hotspot_steps.didYouKnow: Some archaeologists think wooden treads may once have covered the brick steps, but this is uncertain.

hotspot_pool.title: The Great Bath
hotspot_pool.text: This sunken pool, about 12 by 7 metres, is the centrepiece of the citadel. Many scholars suggest it was used for ritual bathing, though this is an interpretation and not a certainty.
hotspot_pool.didYouKnow: A large corbelled drain in one corner carried water out of the pool and into the city's drainage system.

hotspot_bitumen.title: The bitumen lining
hotspot_bitumen.text: The pool's brick floor and walls were made watertight with a layer of natural bitumen sealed between fine-fitted bricks. The dark lining is still visible in places today.
hotspot_bitumen.didYouKnow: Bitumen is a natural tar. Its use here is among the earliest known examples of waterproofing in a large building.

hotspot_corridors.title: The surrounding corridors
hotspot_corridors.text: Covered galleries ringed the pool, giving shade and privacy. Rooms and a staircase hint at additional spaces around the bath.
hotspot_corridors.didYouKnow: Wooden beams, now decayed, probably supported the roof, so our reconstruction here is partly educated guesswork.

hotspot_granary.title: The 'Granary' platform
hotspot_granary.text: A massive brick base is divided by narrow channels, which could have allowed air to circulate. It is traditionally called a granary, but scholars disagree about whether it really held grain.
hotspot_granary.didYouKnow: Little evidence of stored grain has been found, which is one reason the name is debated.

enter.title: Merchant
enter.text: Welcome, traveller! I'm Ravi, and this is our great bazaar. Wander down the street and see how we trade pots, beads, grain, cloth and copper. Step up to a glowing marker and the traders will happily tell you all about their work.
enter.didYouKnow: This street is a reconstruction. No market has been clearly identified at Mohenjo-daro, so the layout is imagined from the crafts and goods archaeologists have found.

tour_street.title: Merchant
tour_street.text: Come along, I'll show you around! Our shops stand shoulder to shoulder, built of baked brick with flat roofs. The awnings keep the sun off the goods.

tour_pottery.title: Potter
tour_pottery.text: Come closer, friend! I'm Dhruv, and clay is my whole life. I throw every pot on the wheel and fire it in the kiln. Many are painted red and black, with patterns of fish scales and leaves.
tour_pottery.didYouKnow: Tiny toy carts and animals made of clay have also been found, so potters probably made playthings too.

tour_beads.title: Bead-maker
tour_beads.text: Oh, a visitor! I'm Samar, the bead-maker, and these are my little treasures. Carnelian, lapis lazuli, shell and faience, all cut, ground and drilled by hand. People wear them as necklaces and bangles.
tour_beads.didYouKnow: Some Indus beads are only a couple of millimetres wide, yet have a hole drilled all the way through.

tour_grain.title: Grain merchant
tour_grain.text: Good day to you! Tarun here, the grain merchant. Wheat and barley, fresh from the fields. I measure it out from these baskets, because a city this size needs a lot of grain.
tour_grain.didYouKnow: Remains of wheat, barley, peas and sesame have been found at Indus sites.

tour_textile.title: Cloth seller
tour_textile.text: Do come and feel this! I'm Lakshmi, and I sell cloth. It's soft cotton, and some of it is dyed red with madder root. I sell it by the length.
tour_textile.didYouKnow: Some of the earliest evidence for cotton cloth in the world comes from the Indus Valley.

tour_weights.title: Trader with scales
tour_weights.text: Step right up! I'm Vihan, and I keep the scales honest. Our stone cubes come in a regular set of sizes. So a trader here and a trader far away can agree on a price.
tour_weights.didYouKnow: Weights found across a huge area follow the same system, a sign of shared standards.

tour_kiln.title: Potter at the kiln
tour_kiln.text: Mind the fire, friend! I'm Kaveri, the potter who tends this kiln. The fire burns below and the pots are stacked above. We build kilns at the edge of town because of all the smoke.
tour_kiln.didYouKnow: Brick kilns like this could reach very high temperatures.

hotspot_seals.title: Trader
hotspot_seals.text: Ah, you have a keen eye! I'm Ishaan, and I trade in little seals. They're carved from soft steatite with an animal and a line of signs. Press one into clay to mark your goods as yours. Nobody today can read the signs!
hotspot_seals.didYouKnow: The Indus script has not yet been deciphered.

hotspot_carts.title: Cart driver
hotspot_carts.text: Easy now, my oxen! I'm Gopal, and I drive this cart. We carry grain, pots, stone and metal along the roads. Boats carry our goods too, and traders take them as far as Mesopotamia.
hotspot_carts.didYouKnow: Clay models of carts with solid wheels look very like carts still used in South Asia today.
